detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: Mill claims that women who have ruled have shown real ability, and that this is a matter of fact rather than inference. He first notes that history shows far fewer reigning queens than kings, yet a far larger proportion of the queens showed talent for rule, often in difficult periods. They were also noted for firmness and vigour as well as intelligence, which runs against the conventional picture of women's character. Adding regents and viceroys of provinces makes the list of eminent women rulers very long (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He says it is certain that a woman can be a Queen Elizabeth, a Deborah, or a Joan of Arc, because that is fact (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He rejects the jibe that men really govern under queens. In his view most great queens were great by their own talents for government and were well served for that reason. If they had good advisers, that shows their judgment suited them to the great questions of government (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). As examples of women ruling well, he cites two princesses who ruled for French kings and the Governors of the Netherlands under Charles V. One of them, Margaret of Austria, he calls one of the ablest politicians of her age (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). From his own official knowledge of Hindoo governments, he reports that well-governed principalities were under a woman's rule in three cases out of four. These women were regents during an heir's minority, and he calls this a striking example of women's natural capacity for government (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He generalizes that where women's capacities for government have been tried, they have been found adequate in that proportion. He attributes this to women of reigning families being allowed the same range of interests and freedom as men (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says power, as he is considering it, is "two-fold": being able to make a change, and being able to receive a change. The first he calls active power and the second passive power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Whenever we observe a change, the mind must infer both a power somewhere able to make it (active) and a possibility in the thing itself to receive it (passive) (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

He adds that sensible things give us plenty of ideas of passive power, since their qualities are in continual flux. He says active power is the "more proper signification" of the word power (same §4 passage). He also holds that bodies give us only an obscure idea of active power. A moving ball, for example, merely transfers received motion rather than producing it. That motion is "rather a passion than an action" in the ball. So the clearest idea of active power comes from reflection on the operations of our own minds (same §4 passage).

A related terminological point appears in Book II, Chapter 22. The efficacy by which an effect is produced is called ACTION in the subject exerting the power, but PASSION in the subject in which an idea is changed or produced (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 22, §11, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Locke is tentative about how these powers are distributed. He says it "may be worth consideration" whether matter is wholly without active power, whether God is above all passive power, and whether created spirits alone are capable of both. He declines to pursue this, because his business is how we come by the idea of power, not its origin. He also suggests that what we commonly call active powers in natural substances may not be so truly active as our hasty thoughts suppose, and he directs us to God and spirits for the clearest idea of active power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Mill claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated?
detail.premise: Mill claims that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated.

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
The passages do not support the premise. Mill does not claim that people always think only of their own pain when their sense of justice is violated. He rejects that as an objection to his view. He says it is no objection to his doctrine that, when we feel our sentiment of justice outraged, we seem to be thinking only of the individual case and not of society (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

Mill does concede that some resentment is purely self-centred. He calls it common, though "the reverse of commendable," to resent something merely because we have suffered pain (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). A person whose resentment is a genuine moral feeling first considers whether an act is blameable. Such a person, even without saying so, feels they are asserting a rule that benefits others as well as themselves. If someone regards the act solely as it affects them individually, Mill says they are not consciously just (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

Mill also explains why the sentiment can look purely personal. Its root is a natural feeling of retaliation, which tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever is disagreeable to us. This feeling is moralized when it is subordinated to the social sympathies, so that just persons resent hurts to society and do not resent merely personal hurts unless society shares an interest in repressing them (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). In his summary, the sentiment is the animal desire to retaliate a hurt to oneself or to those one sympathizes with, widened to include all persons by enlarged sympathy and intelligent self-interest. The animal element gives it its energy, and the widened element gives it its morality (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Hobbes distinguish between justice in people and justice in actions?

expected.author: Thomas Hobbes
expected.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Thomas Hobbes
top_retrieved.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Hobbes holds that "Just" and "Unjust" mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Applied to men, they signify the conformity or inconformity of manners to reason. Applied to actions, they signify conformity or inconformity to reason not of a manner of life but of particular actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called Righteous and Unrighteous, though the meaning is the same (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

The practical consequence is that a man's character does not change with a single act. A righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistake about things or persons. An unrighteous man does not lose his character through actions he does, or refrains from, out of fear, because his will is framed not by justice but by the apparent benefit of what he is to do (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

What gives actions the "relish of Justice" is a certain noblenesse or gallantnesse of courage, rarely found. By it a man scorns to depend for the contentment of his life on fraud or breach of promise. Hobbes says this justice of manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke urges his countrymen to hold up the British Constitution as an example to the French, rather than take French models to improve their own. He calls it "an invaluable treasure" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)).

He credits England's happy situation to the whole Constitution, not to any single part. That includes what earlier reviews and reformations left standing, as well as what was altered or added (same passage). He says his countrymen will find enough work for a patriotic, free and independent spirit in guarding what they possess from violation (same passage).

Burke does not rule out alteration. But even when he changed something, it should be in order to preserve, prompted by a great grievance, and following the example of the ancestors. Repairs should be made as nearly as possible "in the style of the building" (same passage). He recommends imitating the caution of the forefathers, who acted from a sense of human ignorance and fallibility. In his words: add if we please, but preserve what they left, and be content to admire rather than follow "the aëronauts of France" in their desperate flights (same passage).

He also wants the English to keep cherishing the true principles of their own domestic laws. He warns both sides of the water against being imposed on by counterfeit goods sold as British but "manufactured after the newest Paris fashion of an improved liberty" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). He is alarmed by the spirit of change and the contempt for ancient institutions (same passage).

The passages do not give more detailed, practical instructions beyond this general stance of preserving, guarding and cautiously reforming.

detail.answer:
Burke says the British people should take seriously, as a "domestic interest of some moment," how solid the only principle on which the preacher and his associates accept a king of Great Britain as entitled to allegiance (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). The preacher says the king is "almost the only lawful king in the world" because he alone owes his crown to the choice of his people. Burke treats the fate of other kings as their own concern, but the question for Britons is the soundness of this principle (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 21 (edition-specific)).

His worries are these:

1. The claim is false as a matter of fact, and the doctrine is dangerous. Burke says the king does not owe his crown to popular election. So by the preacher's rule he would be no better than the other "usurpers" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

2. The doctrine is a concealed general principle. Burke suggests its promoters hope the abstract principle, that popular choice is necessary for lawful sovereignty, will pass unnoticed while the British king seems unaffected. Meanwhile audiences would grow used to it as an accepted first principle. This would remove the security that British government shares with all governments, so far as opinion is security (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

3. If challenged, the preacher's followers may evade by saying that some past kings were chosen in some way. Burke replies that this would make their idea of election no different from the British idea of inheritance. He adds that the king reigns by a fixed rule of succession under the laws of his country (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). Even so, he says, the explicit declaration of a right in the people to choose cannot be evaded (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

4. The maxim threatens past authority and law. If no throne is lawful unless elective, the acts of earlier princes would be invalid. That would stain the throne with continual usurpation and call into question statute law that protects liberty, such as the Petition of Right and Habeas Corpus (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 43 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Mill treats trade as a social act, so in principle it falls within society's jurisdiction (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He then separates interferences with trade into kinds, depending mainly on whether the principle of individual liberty is really at stake.

1. Interferences that do not truly involve liberty. Restrictions on trade or production for trade are restraints, and "all restraint, quâ restraint, is an evil." But they affect only the part of conduct that society is competent to restrain. They are wrong solely because they fail to produce the results intended, which is the ground of the doctrine of Free Trade (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Mill says that this doctrine rests on grounds different from the liberty principle. The same holds for most questions about the limits of free trade, such as public control to prevent fraud by adulteration, sanitary precautions, or protections for workers in dangerous occupations. Liberty enters only in that leaving people alone is, other things equal, better than controlling them. Mill says that controlling them for these ends is in principle undeniably legitimate (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

2. Interferences that are essentially questions of liberty. These are cases where the aim is to make a commodity impossible or hard to obtain. Mill's examples are the Maine Law, the prohibition of opium imports into China, and restrictions on the sale of poisons. He says they are objectionable not as infringements on the liberty of the producer or seller, but on that of the buyer (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. A further class concerns helping rather than restraining. Here the reasons against interference do not turn on liberty. The question is whether government should do something for people's benefit instead of leaving it to individuals or voluntary combination (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Mill says objections to such interference may be of three kinds (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The first is that individuals are likely to do the thing better, which condemns government interference with ordinary processes of industry (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The third, which he calls the most cogent, is the evil of unnecessarily adding to government power (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)). The passages provided do not include the second objection.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
No. Mill holds that society should not punish people for purely self-regarding faults such as imprudence or lack of personal dignity, though he allows some qualifications.

**Distaste, not punishment.** Mill distinguishes the "loss of consideration" a person may rightly incur through "defect of prudence or of personal dignity" from the reprobation due to an offence against others' rights (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). For self-regarding faults, others may express distaste and stand aloof, but should not try to make the person's life uncomfortable. Because the person already bears the penalty of his own error, we should try to alleviate it rather than add to it. He may be an object of pity or dislike, but not of anger or resentment (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Punishment for the express purpose of punishing is reserved for those who infringe the rules protecting others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

**The general maxim.** The individual is not accountable to society for actions that concern only himself. Advice, instruction, persuasion and avoidance are the only justified ways of expressing disapproval. Punishment, social or legal, is justified for actions prejudicial to others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

**Objections Mill rejects.** He sets out the argument that society should protect adults who are unfit for self-government, and should repress gambling, drunkenness, idleness and similar vices, through law or through social penalties (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He also sets out the argument that no one is isolated, so self-injury harms others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). His reply is that the merely contingent or "constructive" injury to society from such conduct is an inconvenience society can bear for the sake of the greater good of human freedom (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Society has had the whole period of childhood to make people capable of rational conduct, and should not wait until they act irrationally and then punish them (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Coercion also tends to backfire: independent characters will rebel against it (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Mill says the bad example of self-regarding misconduct is likely, on the whole, to be more salutary than hurtful, because it also displays the painful consequences (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

**Qualifications.** When a person's conduct breaks a distinct, assignable obligation to others, it is no longer purely self-regarding. A man who cannot support his family or pay his debts because of intemperance or extravagance may justly be punished, but for the breach of duty, not for the extravagance (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Drunkenness is ordinarily not a fit subject for legislation, but a person previously convicted of violence while drunk may be placed under a special restriction. Idleness cannot be punished without tyranny, except where the person is publicly supported or has breached a contract or legal duty to others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a source of government. Governments originally arise only from the consent of the people, but the noise of war has led many to "mistake the force of arms for the consent of the people" and to count conquest as an original of government (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says conquest is as far from setting up a government "as demolishing an house is from building a new one in the place." It may often make way for a new commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

This fits his wider claim that, as far as history gives light, all peaceful beginnings of government were laid in the consent of the people. He explicitly says "peaceful" because he reserves conquest for separate discussion, noting that some esteem it a way of beginning governments (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §112, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He also holds that governments begun in peace were founded on consent (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §104, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

Locke also limits what a conqueror gains. A conqueror gets no power over those who conquered alongside him. Their descendants are freemen, not subjects by conquest, and he applies this to the claim that the English monarchy rests on the Norman conquest (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Even if the conqueror's war were just, damage suffered between men in the state of nature cannot let him dispossess the posterity of the vanquished. Otherwise, conquest gives only the title bare force gives the stronger over the weaker, so that the strongest would have a right to whatever he pleases to seize (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Finally, even if a conqueror did have a right to the conquered's estates (which Locke says he does not), no absolute power would follow. The descendants are freemen, and whatever the conqueror grants them becomes their property, which cannot be taken without their own consent (Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give Locke's full account of conquest, such as when a war is just, beyond these points.

detail.answer:
Burke thinks the ministers' position is both perilous and degrading, for several reasons given in the passages.

1. **No glory, only peril.** Burke contrasts France with other countries: elsewhere the office of minister of state is "of the highest dignity," but in France it is "full of peril, and incapable of glory" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

2. **Open to attack, unable to answer properly.** Rivals can, under the Constitution, attack the ministers in their vital parts. The ministers can reply only in the "degrading character of culprits." Burke adds that they are the only people in France who cannot share in the national councils (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

3. **Responsibility without active service.** Burke grants that responsibility prevents crimes. But he says it is a poor basis for "active and zealous service," and that the "elevation of mind to be derived from fear will never make a nation glorious" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

4. **Servitude under two masters.** Burke says the ministers are in a "subordinate servitude" never seen before. They lack the confidence of the king, on whom they were forced, and of the Assembly, which forced them on him. The Assembly's committees carry out the noble functions of their office regardless of the ministers' authority. They must "execute, without power," be "responsible, without discretion," and "deliberate, without choice." Standing between two sovereigns, over neither of whom they have influence, they must sometimes betray one, sometimes the other, and always themselves (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

5. **Witnessing the damage.** Burke says that from their "eminence of humiliation" they were the first to see and feel the evils the Revolution produced. They also felt their country's degraded state and their own "utter incapacity of serving it." He is astonished they have not resigned already and says he would not have stood in their place (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

Burke's claim that the ministers wished the Revolution well is hedged ("I take it for granted"), so he does not present it as certain. The passages do not say more about individual ministers beyond this.

detail.answer:
The question's premise is mistaken: the passages show Locke arguing the opposite, that private property is justified, including in the earliest ages. He starts from the view that God gave the earth to mankind in common, and says he will show "how men might come to have a property in several parts" of it without any express compact of all the commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His answer is labour. Because a man is master of himself and proprietor of his own person and its labour, he had "the great foundation of property" in himself (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §44, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). Labour in the beginning gave a right of property whenever someone employed it on what was common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). Locke's examples: a deer is the goods of the Indian who killed it, and a hunted hare is the property of whoever pursues it (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §30, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

He also argues that early appropriation harmed no one. Nature set the measure of property by the extent of men's labour and the conveniences of life. No one could appropriate everything or consume more than a small part, so there was still room for others to have "as good, and as large a possession" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Later, communities settled property boundaries by laws and agreement, which settled the property that labour had begun (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

Locke also holds that property should be protected. Men join society for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which he calls by the general name property (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 9, §123, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The supreme power cannot take any part of a man's property without his consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 11, §138, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). The Burke passage is about property in the context of the French Revolution and does not bear on Locke's argument.

detail.answer:
Locke says he is willing to revise his views on liberty and the will, and he reports that he has actually done so. He calls himself "a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines" and says he owns some change of opinion since an earlier edition (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78 (edition-specific)). He says he does not fancy himself infallible and will not hide his mistakes to protect his reputation, so he is not ashamed to publish what a "severer inquiry" suggested (same passage). He accepts that some readers may prefer his former notions, some the later ones, and some neither. He would be grateful to anyone who could clear the subject of remaining difficulties (same passage).

In the Epistle to the Reader he says that on closer inspection he found reason to alter his earlier thoughts about what gives the last determination to the Will in voluntary actions. He acknowledges this freely, thinking himself more concerned to renounce his own opinion than to oppose another's when truth is against it. He adds that it is truth alone he seeks (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

He qualifies this. He is ready to give up any opinion on the first evidence of error, yet he says the objections printed against his book have given him no light and no reason to change his view on the questioned points (same Epistle passage).

In Chapter 21 he explains how the revision came about. He himself feared the chapter had a mistake, and a judicious friend suspected one without being able to point to it. This led him to a stricter review, in which he found a "very easy and scarce observable slip", namely putting one seemingly indifferent word for another. That discovery gave him the new view he submits in the second edition (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 77 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the word Church (Latin Ecclesia) "signifieth in the Books of Holy Scripture divers things" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He lists these senses:

1. A house or temple. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's House, a Temple where Christians gather for public holy duties. Hobbes says this use is metaphorical, standing for the congregation assembled there, and was later applied to the building itself to distinguish Christian temples from those of idolaters. He traces the English word to the Greek Kuriake, "The Lords House" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. A congregation or assembly of citizens. When not meaning a house, Church means what Ecclesia meant in the Grecian Common-wealths: citizens called forth to hear the magistrate speak. If called by lawful authority it was a lawful Church (Ecclesia Legitima). If stirred up by tumultuous and seditious clamor, it was a confused Church (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. Other scriptural uses (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)):
- The men who have a right to be of the Congregation, though not actually assembled, meaning all Christians however dispersed. Hobbes cites Saul making havoc of the Church, and Christ as Head of the Church.
- A certain part of Christians, as in "Salute the Church that is in his house."
- The Elect only, meaning the Church Triumphant or Church To Come.
- A congregation of professors of Christianity, whether their profession is true or counterfeit, as in "Tell it to the Church."

4. One Person. Hobbes says only in the last sense (an assembled congregation) can the Church be taken as one Person that can will, command, make laws or act. This requires authority from a lawful Congregation. He defines a Church as "a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign," who commands when they assemble (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, In What Sense The Church Is One Person Church Defined, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: The question's premise does not match the Hobbes passages provided. Hobbes does not argue that the sovereign should never regulate opinions and doctrines. He argues the opposite. He says it is annexed to the Sovereignty (attached to the sovereign's office) to judge which opinions and doctrines are averse to peace and which conduce to it, and to examine the doctrines of books before they are published (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). His reasoning is that men's actions proceed from their opinions. Governing opinions well is therefore how actions are governed well, for the sake of peace and concord (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He holds that a doctrine repugnant to peace cannot be true, just as peace cannot be against the Law of Nature. He concludes that the sovereign should be judge, or appoint all judges, of opinions and doctrines to prevent discord and civil war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). Hobbes also warns against private conscience as a rule. In a commonwealth, he says, the Law is the publique Conscience, and private consciences are only private opinions. If each person followed his own, the commonwealth would be distracted and no one would obey the sovereign beyond what seemed good in his own eyes (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 29, Erroneous Conscience, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). The view that a government should never control opinion appears in John Stuart Mill, not Hobbes. Mill calls such coercion illegitimate (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He also argues that the usefulness of an opinion is itself a matter of opinion (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). The passages give no Hobbesian argument against sovereign regulation of doctrines.

detail.answer:
For Hobbes, a sin is broader than a crime: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

**Sin.** A sin is not only a transgression of a law but also any contempt of the legislator, because such contempt breaches all his laws at once. It can therefore lie in a deed, in words, in omitting what the law commands, or even in the intention or purpose to transgress (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Hobbes says that to intend to steal or kill is a sin even if it never shows in word or deed, because God sees thoughts and can charge them to a man (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He does limit this: merely taking pleasure in imagining something is not a sin. The sin begins with resolving to carry out an act that tends toward it (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

**Crime.** A crime is a sin consisting in committing, by deed or word, what the law forbids, or omitting what it commands (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He ties crime to the civil law and sin to law in general (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). The difference is accusability. A crime is the kind of sin of which one man may accuse another, so bare intentions that never appear in an outward act cannot be accused by humans. Hobbes finds this distinction in the Greek words for sin and crime and in the Latin *peccatum* and *crimen*. The Latin *crimen* means only sins that can be made to appear before a judge (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

**Consequences.** Where law ceases, sin ceases. But the law of nature is eternal, so violations of covenants, ingratitude, arrogance and other acts contrary to moral virtue never cease to be sin. When civil law ceases, crimes cease, since only the law of nature remains. Then there is no place for accusation, and each man is judged only by his own conscience. A wrong act is then a sin but not a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.premise: Hobbes holds that obeying a sovereign's command to break the law still makes the person guilty before the sovereign.

top_retrieved.author: Thomas Hobbes

top_retrieved.author: Thomas Hobbes
top_retrieved.locator: Part II, Chapter 27, Totall Excuses, paragraph 25 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
The passages do not directly discuss a sovereign who expressly commands a subject to break the law. They address a close case, where the law-maker condemns an act in the law but shows by "other manifest signes" that he tacitly (silently) approves it. Hobbes treats this as a lesser crime than an act condemned by both law and law-maker (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)).

The reasoning is as follows. Because the law-maker's will is itself a law, the case contains two contradictory laws (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). Hobbes says this would totally excuse the subject if men were bound to take notice of the sovereign's approval through arguments other than what his command expresses (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). I read this to mean that men are not so bound, so the subject is not wholly excused. That is an inference from the conditional wording, not something Hobbes states outright. The subject therefore stays guilty, though the guilt is reduced.

The guilt is reduced because the sovereign attaches punishments to observing the law as well as to breaking it. This makes him "in part a cause of the transgression", so he cannot fairly put the whole crime on the offender (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). Hobbes's example is the duel. The law punishes duelling with death, but a man who refuses a duel faces contempt and is sometimes judged unfit for military office by the sovereign himself. Such a man should not be punished rigorously, since part of the fault falls on the punisher (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). Hobbes adds that he does not intend this to license private revenge or any other disobedience, but to urge governors not to indirectly encourage what they directly forbid (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)).

The passages leave unanswered how Hobbes would treat an explicit sovereign command to break the law, and they do not state the guilt-before-the-sovereign claim in those terms.

detail.question: According to Locke, why does the bond between male and female animals sometimes last beyond mating?

expected.author: John Locke
expected.locator: Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: John Locke
top_retrieved.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2

detail.answer:
For Locke, the bond lasts beyond mating when the young still need support. He says the purpose of the union between male and female is "not barely procreation, but the continuation of the species," so it ought to last after procreation "so long as is necessary to the nourishment and support of the young ones" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He treats this as a rule set by the "infinite wise maker" that the lower creatures steadily obey (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

He gives examples of how this varies:
- In grass-eating viviparous animals (those that bear live young), the bond lasts only as long as copulation. The mother's teat is enough to nourish the young until they can feed on grass, and the male can contribute nothing to their sustenance (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).
- In beasts of prey the bond lasts longer. The mother cannot easily support herself and her numerous offspring by her own prey alone, so the male's help is necessary until the young can prey for themselves (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).
- In birds the young need food in the nest, so cock and hen stay mates until the young can use their wings and provide for themselves. Locke makes an exception for some domestic birds, where plentiful food excuses the cock from feeding and caring for the brood (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Where the young can subsist on their own before the time of procreation returns, the conjugal bond dissolves of itself and the animals are free to choose new mates (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Locke applies the same reasoning to humans, whose bond is longer for a related reason. The woman usually conceives again and bears another child long before the earlier one can fend for itself, so the father must stay in conjugal society longer (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke raises several concerns about how the Assembly handled the finances of the confiscated Church lands. The passages support the following points.

1. The fund was burdened with new charges. The confiscated lands were supposed to show a surplus free of all charges. The Assembly instead loaded onto them compensation for the disbanded judicature and for suppressed offices and estates, which Burke says unquestionably comes to many French millions. They also added an annuity of 480,000 pounds sterling for the interest on the first assignats (the paper currency issued against the lands) (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

2. The cost of management was never fairly stated. Burke asks whether the Assembly ever stated the expense of managing the Church lands. They left the lands to the municipalities and their "legion of unknown under-agents" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

3. The planners lacked competence. Burke says those who took on the role of financier of confiscation were bound to show that they understood the office. Their task was to make their bank a real fund of credit, so far as such a bank could be one (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 401 (edition-specific)). He also asks who but desperate adventurers would destroy the settled revenue of the state, the sole security for public credit, to rebuild it from confiscated property (same passage).

4. A sudden sale would have defeated its own purpose. Putting this huge mass of land on the market at once would depreciate the value of those lands and of all landed estates in France. It would also divert circulating money from trade to land (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 219 (edition-specific)). Burke describes the Assembly's shifting schemes as the result of difficulties and of public pressure on all sides, including the Minister of Finance's urgent calls for supply (same passage).

5. The terms of sale amounted to selling to buyers without money. Only part of the purchase price was to be paid up front, with twelve years allowed for the rest. Burke says this makes the sale "in some respects a sort of gift" and lets in "a body of purchasers without money" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 222 (edition-specific)). He expects these grantees to pay out of rents, which the state might as well have collected. They would also draw on the spoil of buildings, waste in woods, and whatever they could extract from the peasant (same passage).

The passages do not give a full accounting of the actual figures. Burke himself says he cannot ascertain the total of the new charges (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What misconception about the meaning of 'utility' does Mill address in this paragraph?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: In this paragraph Mill addresses the mistaken belief that "utility" is opposed to pleasure. He calls this an "ignorant blunder" and says those who defend utility as the test of right and wrong do not use the word in the "restricted and merely colloquial sense in which utility is opposed to pleasure" (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He notes the irony that utilitarianism is also accused of the opposite fault, referring everything to pleasure in its grossest form, so that the same people call it "impracticably dry" when utility comes before pleasure and "too practicably voluptuous" when pleasure comes first (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). According to Mill, every writer from Epicurus to Bentham who held the theory meant by utility pleasure itself, together with exemption from pain, not something set against pleasure. These writers declared that the useful includes the agreeable and the ornamental among other things (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Mill says the common herd, including writers, take up the word "utilitarian" knowing only its sound and use it to mean rejection or neglect of pleasure, such as beauty, ornament or amusement. The term is sometimes misapplied as a compliment, as though it implied superiority to frivolity, and Mill calls this perverted use the only one in which the word is popularly known (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passage breaks off mid-sentence, so what Mill says next is not covered here.

detail.answer:
Burke objects mainly because he thinks constant talk of resistance and revolution is unhealthy for society and misuses the principles of the Revolution it claims to honor. The main points are below.

1. **It cheats people of the Revolution's benefits.** He fears the anniversary sermons will "cheat many out of the principles and deprive them of the benefits of the Revolution they commemorate." He says he never liked "this continual talk of resistance and revolution," or the habit of making "the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread." This, he says, makes society dangerously "valetudinary" (sickly, prone to ill health). He compares it to taking regular doses of poison and stimulants to our love of liberty (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)).

2. **It hardens the moral sentiments for no purpose.** He says the worst of the "politics of revolution" is that they "temper and harden the breast" for desperate strokes that may be needed only on extreme occasions. If those occasions never come, the mind gets a "gratuitous taint" and moral sentiments suffer with no political purpose served. He adds that such people are so absorbed in theories of the rights of man that they forget his nature (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 114 (edition-specific)).

3. **It spreads a spirit of change and contempt for ancient institutions.** He dislikes revolutions whose signals are so often given from pulpits. He ties this to the spreading "spirit of change" and a contempt for ancient institutions when they are set against present convenience or inclination (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

4. **It misreads the 1688 settlement.** He says the caution of the earlier Revolution's framers shows they wanted it to be "a parent of settlement, and not a nursery of future revolutions." Celebrating revolution as a standing right runs against that intent (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 49 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not say more about the anniversary sermons beyond these points.

detail.answer:
Burke argues that the new French Constitution severs the link between the people and their representatives. He says that "there is little, or rather no, connection between the last representative and the first constituent." In his account, a member of the National Assembly "is not chosen by the people, nor accountable to them" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)). Three elections, with two sets of magistracy between him and the primary assembly, make him "an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state." Burke adds that, unless the people break up and level this gradation, "they do not at all substantially elect to the Assembly" (same, paragraph 326). He also says that any corrective would only plunge the system back into the tumult of popular election, which the gradation was meant to avoid. He calls this a "perpetual dilemma" caused by the "vicious, weak, and contradictory principles" chosen (same, paragraph 326).

Burke links this to the structure of the Assembly. He describes it as in effect a general congress of ambassadors from independent republics, with no constitutional means of coherence or subordination beyond their acquiescence in its decisions (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 318 (edition-specific)). He contrasts this with Britain. There the representative, "separated from the other parts, can have no action and no existence," and the government is a trustee "for the whole, and not for the parts." In France, by contrast, "the elective Assembly is the sovereign, and the sole sovereign" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 325 (edition-specific)).

Burke also doubts that numbers alone make a government legitimate or good. He says the will and the interest of the many "must very often differ," and that a government of obscure attorneys and curates is not good for twenty-four millions even if chosen by many more (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 93 (edition-specific)). He predicts the Constitution will end in rule by an "ignoble oligarchy" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 339 (edition-specific)).
